title: Biomass Organs Control the Porosity of Their Pyrolyzed Carbon

nodes.label: Organs of one plant differ in embedded alkali content; the alkali-richer organ should pyrolyze to more porous carbon without added activator
Use lotus stems and leaves as feedstock: stems carry water and salts, leaves make organics
Compare stem vs leaf carbons, pyrolysis 500-900 C (lotus), extended to celery and asparagus lettuce
Wash and freeze-dry lotus stems and leaves as carbon feedstock

attrs.note: feedstock preparation; closest PRC leaf (no reaction, feedstock kept intact)

nodes.label: Stems hold more total metal than leaves, K dominant and about 3x higher (~2.5 vs ~0.9 g/100 g)

attrs.image_note: Ca, Mg and (marginally) Zn are higher in the leaf; total, K, Na, Al, Fe, Cu higher in stem

nodes.label: Pyrolyze organs under N2 (800 C, 3 h; 500-1100 C in sweeps), then wash, giving S-, L-, WS-, WL-carbon
Leach metals from freeze-dried organs with 1 M HCl before carbonization to isolate the alkali effect
Wash freeze-dried stems and leaves in 1 M HCl, removing most metals and acid-soluble organics
Molecularly embedded K salts decompose at 200-500 C and etch carbon at 500-800 C during densification, creating micro- and mesopores

requires_unseen: assignment of the extra 500-800 C mass loss to salt etching

nodes.label: S-carbon has ~50% higher BET area than L-carbon (1610 vs 1039 m2/g) with more micro- and mesopores
WS- and WL-carbon have near-identical, lower areas (803 and 909 m2/g) and no mesopore peak

attrs.image_note: grayscale legend does not let one tell which dashed curve is 909 vs 803

nodes.label: The S- vs L-carbon area difference is set by the organs' embedded alkali content, not by organ morphology or carbon chemistry

requires_unseen: HCl wash removed most metals from the organs (ICP, Table S2)

nodes.label: Stem-derived carbons of celery and asparagus lettuce also exceed leaf carbons in area (CS 1230-2120 vs CL 330-570; AS 1075 vs AL 735 m2/g)

requires_unseen: CS/CL = celery stem/leaf, AS/AL = asparagus lettuce stem/leaf (caption)

nodes.label: S-carbon delivers higher specific capacitance than L-carbon at every scan rate (~174 vs ~152 F/g at 5 mV/s)
S-carbon symmetric supercapacitor keeps ~100% capacitance over 10 000 charge-discharge cycles at 1 A/g

requires_unseen: cell is symmetric S-carbon supercapacitor at 1 A/g (caption)

nodes.label: The organ's embedded alkali (K) content controls porosity and capacitance of pyrolyzed biomass carbon; stems beat leaves in three plants
Both carbons are amorphous and highly disordered with near-equal graphitization (broad (002)/(101) humps, ID/IG ~1.19 vs 1.17)
Both carbons consist of C and O only, with similar O 1s signal (surface oxygen groups)
Carbons inherit organ morphology: stem honeycomb channels and leaf mesophyll flakes are preserved
Celery and asparagus lettuce stems also hold more total metal and K than their leaves
S-carbon keeps 72% of capacitance at 500 mV/s vs 64% for L-carbon
S-carbon stores charge capacitively: near-rectangular CVs with no redox peaks from 5 to 500 mV/s
AS-carbon capacitance exceeds AL-carbon (~155 vs ~102 F/g at 5 mV/s), tracking their areas
Area does not set capacitance in celery: CL-carbon lacks micropores yet reaches 85% of CS-carbon, with areal capacitance 39.4 uF/cm2
Naturally contained alkalis activate biomass during carbonization and create porosity [33,36-41]
Raman D band ~1340 cm-1 marks defects, G ~1585 cm-1 graphitic carbon; broad (002)/(101) humps mean amorphous carbon
Only part of the pore surface stores ions; meso- and macropores serve high rates [46-49]
Theoretical double-layer capacitance of carbon is ~21 uF/cm2
Near-rectangular CV without redox peaks is the signature of double-layer capacitance

ICP bars for two more plants: stem exceeds leaf in total metal and K; most minor metals higher in leaf
